evidence.title: Night Kitchen — shared commercial kitchen hours for street-food vendors
evidence.problem: Licensed street-food vendors in mid-size Texas cities need a certified commercial kitchen to prep legally, but commissary kitchens are rented by the month at prices built for restaurants. Vendors working three nights a week pay for hours they never use or prep at home and risk their permit.
evidence.solution: Night Kitchen rents certified commissary kitchens by the hour between 10pm and 6am, when restaurant kitchens sit idle. We handle scheduling, access control and the health-department paper trail; the host restaurant earns rent on dead hours.
evidence.market: There are roughly 1,400 permitted mobile food vendors across Austin, San Antonio and Dallas. Most rent commissary access at 400 to 900 dollars a month. We charge 18 dollars an hour with a 10 hour monthly minimum.
evidence.business_model: Hourly fee split 70/30 with the host kitchen. Vendors prepay a block of hours; hosts are paid out weekly.
evidence.traction: Two host kitchens signed letters of intent in Austin. Twelve vendors on a waitlist from one weekend at a night market. No revenue yet.
evidence.competition: Monthly commissaries, ghost-kitchen operators who want full-time tenants, and informal home prep.
evidence.team: One founder who ran a food truck for four years and holds a current food-manager certification. Looking for a technical co-founder.
evidence.risks: Health-department acceptance of shared overnight use; host kitchens pulling out if cleanup is poor; insurance.
evidence.ask: An honest assessment of whether this is worth building before I quit my day job.

goal.founder_question: Is this worth building before I quit my day job?
